Emerging during a transformative epoch of decolonization and constitutional restructuring within the Dutch Empire, she shattered gender barriers to become the first female Prime Minister of the Netherlands Antilles. Her career spanned decades of dedicated public service, marked by profound contributions to public health, environmental welfare, youth empowerment, and the advancement of women's rights across Curaçao and its sister islands. Operating within a complex political landscape dominated by colonial legacies and male leadership, da Costa Gomez-Matheeuws demonstrated exceptional diplomatic acumen and legislative pragmatism. As a core leader of the National People's Party (",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Partido Nacional di Pueblo"}]," or PNP), she helped navigate the Netherlands Antilles through turbulent socio-economic transitions, establishing a progressive framework for social welfare that continues to influence Caribbean governance today [1]."]}],"\n",["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"Early Life and Professional Beginnings"}],"\n",["$","p","p-1",{"children":["Born on April 5, 1929, in Willemstad, Curaçao, Lucina Matheeuws came of age during a period of intense rapid modernization on the island. The establishment and expansion of the Royal Dutch Shell oil refinery had transformed Curaçao from a quiet colonial outpost into a bustling, diverse industrial hub of the Caribbean. This economic boom brought significant migration, labor dynamism, and growing calls for political representation among the local population, who remained disenfranchised under traditional colonial structures. Educated locally in Willemstad, Matheeuws exhibited early academic excellence and a rigorous flair for administrative organization. Entering government service as a young woman—a rare career trajectory for women of her generation—she secured a position at the Secretariat of the Court of Justice. Her sharp analytical skills and professionalism quickly earned her promotions, leading to her appointment as secretary to the chairman of the Government Council (","$L9","), the executive administrative body of the island before full autonomous governance was realized [3]. Working at the very nerve center of colonial administration provided Matheeuws with an unparalleled, firsthand education in jurisprudence, public administration, and legislative drafting, sowing the seeds for her future leadership."]}],"\n","$La","\n","$Lb","\n","$Lc","\n","$Ld","\n","$Le","\n","$Lf","\n","$L10","\n","$L11","\n","$L12","\n","$L13","\n","$L14","\n","$L15","\n","$L16","\n","$L17","\n","$L18"]}]]}],"$L19","$L1a",false]}],"$L1b"]}]

a:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":"Political Awakening and Alliance"}]
b:["$","p","p-2",{"children":["During her tenure in government service, Lucina crossed paths with Dr. ",["$","$L1f","a-0",{"slug":"moises-frumencio-da-costa-gomez","href":"/profiles/moises-frumencio-da-costa-gomez","children":"Moises Frumencio da Costa Gomez"}],", a visionary jurist and the undisputed architect of Antillean autonomy. Dr. da Costa Gomez had founded the National People's Party (PNP) in 1948 with the mission of securing self-determination and universal suffrage for the people of the Netherlands Antilles. Their professional collaboration blossomed into a deep intellectual and personal partnership, culminating in their marriage [3]. Becoming Lucina da Costa Gomez-Matheeuws, she found herself at the epicenter of Antillean political evolution. Her husband served as the Chairman of the Governing Council and subsequently as the first Prime Minister of the Netherlands Antilles from 1951 to 1954, successfully negotiating the landmark Charter for the Kingdom of the Netherlands (",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Statuut voor het Koninkrijk der Nederlanden"}],") in 1954 [4]. While Dr. da Costa Gomez was the public face of autonomy, Lucina was a vital strategic confidante, organizational force, and grassroots mobilizer within the PNP. Following her husband's untimely passing in 1966, she did not retreat from public life; instead, she resolved to carry forward their shared vision of democratic empowerment and social equity."]}]
c:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"The Trinta di Mei and Rise to Parliament"}]
d:["$","p","p-3",{"children":["The late 1960s brought unprecedented socio-political upheaval to Curaçao. Despite constitutional autonomy within the Kingdom, economic disparities, racial stratification, and labor exploitation persisted, erupting violently on May 30, 1969, in the historic labor uprising known as ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Trinta di Mei"}]," [3]. The uprising catalyzed the collapse of the government and compelled a radical re-evaluation of Antillean society, demanding authentic grassroots representation and social justice for the Afro-Curaçaoan majority. In the crucible of the subsequent general elections of August 1969, Lucina da Costa Gomez-Matheeuws stood as a beacon of stability and reform for the PNP. Campaigning tirelessly across urban neighborhoods and rural districts, she won a seat as a member of the Staten (Parliament) of the Netherlands Antilles [1]. Her election marked a decisive shift toward inclusive governance. In Parliament, she distinguished herself by bridging polarized political factions and championing legislative measures aimed at alleviating poverty, expanding educational access, and protecting vulnerable workers."]}]
e:["$","p","p-4",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b1/Flag_of_Cura%C3%A7ao.svg","alt":"Flag of Curaçao representing Antillean Autonomy"}]}]
f:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"True autonomy is not merely the shifting of political boundaries or constitutional charters; it is the daily empowerment of our people—especially our women and youth—to shape their own destinies within a just and compassionate society.\" [1]"}],"\n"]}]
10:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"Transformative Ministerial Tenure"}]
11:["$","p","p-5",{"children":"Recognized for her administrative brilliance and deep commitment to social welfare, da Costa Gomez-Matheeuws was appointed Minister of Health and Environment, Welfare, Youth, Sports, Culture, and Recreation in 1970, a robust portfolio she managed with distinction until 1977 [1]. Over these seven years, she engineered a comprehensive modernization of the island's social infrastructure. Recognizing that healthcare was a fundamental human right, she spearheaded initiatives to expand community medical clinics, improve sanitation standards across the islands, and invest in preventative healthcare education [3]. Within the cultural sphere, she actively promoted local arts and fostered national pride by institutionalizing support for indigenous traditions and sports programs for disadvantaged youth."}]
12:["$","p","p-6",{"children":"Crucially, da Costa Gomez-Matheeuws utilized her ministerial authority to advocate for profound legal reforms regarding family law and women's rights. At the time, remnants of archaic colonial legal codes severely restricted married women's economic and legal independence. She tirelessly championed legislative reforms that dismantled these archaic patriarchal provisions, granting women full legal autonomy to enter contracts, manage property, and function independently within society [3]. Her visionary policies laid the groundwork for modern gender equality across Curaçao, Aruba, Bonaire, Sint Maarten, Sint Eustatius, and Saba."}]
13:["$","h3","h3-5",{"children":"Shattering the Glass Ceiling: Prime Minister"}]
14:["$","p","p-7",{"children":["In October 1977, amidst a period of delicate political transition and coalition recalibration, Lucina da Costa Gomez-Matheeuws achieved a historic milestone: she was sworn in as Prime Minister of the Netherlands Antilles (",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"ad interim"}]," from October 4 to October 14, 1977) [1][4]. With this appointment, she became the first woman in the history of the Netherlands Antilles—and indeed within the entire Kingdom of the Netherlands—to lead a government executive [2]. Though her tenure as Prime Minister was brief due to the interim nature of the coalition restructuring, its symbolic and structural impact was monumental. She governed with calm decisiveness, ensuring executive continuity and demonstrating that women could command the highest echelons of state power. Her leadership shattered longstanding Caribbean gender prejudices and established a powerful precedent that directly inspired future female leaders across the region, most notably her PNP colleague ",["$","$L1f","a-0",{"slug":"maria-liberia-peters","href":"/profiles/maria-liberia-peters","children":"Maria Liberia-Peters"}],", who would later serve multiple extended terms as Prime Minister alongside leaders like ",["$","$L1f","a-1",{"slug":"juancho-evertsz","href":"/profiles/juancho-evertsz","children":"Juancho Evertsz"}],"."]}]
15:["$","p","p-8",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/64/Handelskade_Willemstad.jpg","alt":"Historic Handelskade Waterfront in Willemstad"}]}]
16:["$","blockquote","blockquote-1",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"By stepping into the highest political office of the Netherlands Antilles, Lucina da Costa Gomez-Matheeuws permanently dismantled the gendered barriers of Caribbean leadership, proving that the governance of our islands belongs equally to the women who nurture their foundations.\" [2]"}],"\n"]}]
17:["$","h3","h3-6",{"children":"Elder Stateswoman and Lasting Legacy"}]
18:["$","p","p-9",{"children":["Following her departure from active cabinet politics, da Costa Gomez-Matheeuws remained an indispensable intellectual pillar of Curaçaoan public life. She was appointed to the prestigious Council of Advisors (",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Raad van Advies"}],"), the highest independent advisory body to the government and parliament on legislative and constitutional matters [5]. For years, she lent her immense institutional knowledge and legal acumen to reviewing state policies, earning widespread reverence as a revered elder stateswoman. She passed away on January 7, 2017, in Willemstad, at the age of 87, mourned across the Kingdom as a matriarch of democratic governance [1]. In tribute to her monumental contributions, the government of Curaçao dedicated a major traffic roundabout near the Renaissance Mall in Willemstad in her honor in 2015 [3]. Her legacy endures not only in the modernized welfare structures of Curaçao but in the vibrant, undeniable presence of women leading Caribbean democracy today."]}]
19:["$","$L20",null,{"title":"Learn about the legacy of Lucina da Costa Gomez-Matheeuws","url":"https://caribbeanlegacyarchive.com/profiles/lucina-da-costa"}]
21:T431,Lucina da Costa Gomez-Matheeuws made groundbreaking contributions to Caribbean governance, gender equality, and social welfare modernization. As the first female Prime Minister of the Netherlands Antilles in 1977, she shattered historical glass ceilings within the Dutch Caribbean and the broader Kingdom of the Netherlands, establishing an enduring precedent for female executive leadership that inspired generations of women in politics.

During her extensive tenure as Minister of Health, Environment, Welfare, Youth, Sports, Culture, and Recreation (1970–1977), she spearheaded transformative legal and institutional reforms. Most notably, she championed progressive marriage and family law reforms that abolished archaic colonial patriarchal codes, legally empowering women to function with full economic and civil independence. Additionally, she expanded public health infrastructure, championed preventive healthcare, and institutionalized state support for cultural and youth development, fundamentally reshaping the social safety net of the Netherlands Antilles.1a:["$","div",null,{"className":"mb-12 pt-12 border-t border-gold/10","children":[["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Major Contributions"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed bg-white p-8 border-l-4 border-tropical-green shadow-sm","children":"$21"}]]}]
